video_title: Can Open Models Keep Up With OpenAI and Anthropic? | Nathan Lambert
gist: Nathan Lambert (launching the nonprofit open lab Trillium) argues open-weight models can stay near the frontier: Chinese labs equal the US on talent but lack compute, distillation is a smaller lever than assumed in today's RL-heavy post-training, and data/environment diffusion makes fast-following easy. He expects tiered markets (closed models with top margins, near-frontier open models), doubts fast takeoff given exponential compute costs, and worries more about societal unpreparedness like cybersecurity.

themes.theme: Capital, org charts and frontier lab cultures

insights.claim: Nathan Lambert frames model progress as a function of three forms of capital (compute, data, talent), with the binding constraint being a lab's ability to organize them via its org chart.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Evaluate labs on organizational execution, not just capital raised.
insights.quote: When I think about model progress, it comes down to like different forms of capital that you put into them. And that is like compute, data, and talent.

insights.claim: Lambert says Meta did a complete bottom-up reset of its AI org and is now on a positive trajectory again.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Meta's model efforts may be re-rating upward after reorganization.
insights.quote: Like company like Meta is like totally reset and they're like on a positive trajectory again.

insights.claim: Lambert's default advice for working at the AI frontier is Anthropic or OpenAI; Meta, Google and SpaceX AI may be there but are harder to judge from outside.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Talent flows and perceived frontier status still concentrate in two labs.
insights.quote: if somebody wants to work at the frontier of AI, I mostly tell them to work at Anthropic and OpenAI, which is the easiest bet, I think.

insights.claim: OpenAI's culture excels at paradigm-shifting breakthroughs like the reasoning-model/inference-scaling plot, while Anthropic's long focus on what models can do in coding was rewarded by the Claude Code explosion.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Distinct lab cultures produce distinct product wins; coding was Anthropic's payoff.
insights.quote: their reward was this Claude code explosion with their focus on coding for so long.

insights.claim: Coding has been the story of the year, with associated revenue going from zero to roughly $100 billion and likely to grow, captured first by integrated closed labs.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Coding is the proven high-value market where closed labs' first-mover advantage monetizes.
insights.quote: We have seen this with coding and this has been the story of the year where the revenue has just gone zero 100 billion and likely to grow.

insights.claim: Lambert expected industry consolidation two years ago after ChatGPT, but M&A is only now becoming active and open-model companies have survived longer than he predicted.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: A more active AI M&A cycle is starting now.
insights.quote: I think we're just starting to see a much more active mergers and acquisitions market, but I thought this was going to happen 2 years ago.

insights.claim: Chinese labs release open-weight models as a practical distribution strategy: selling an API from China would leave firms like Moonshot AI or Jipu (Zhipu) unknown, so open weights get them into the US conversation and market.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Chinese open releases are go-to-market, not altruism or state directive.
insights.quote: releasing open models is a way to shortcut this and get into the conversation.

insights.claim: Lambert argues China is equal to the US on AI talent; the decisive gap is compute, illustrated by a top Chinese pretraining researcher being stunned that an average OpenAI researcher has ~5,000 H100 equivalents available.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Compute access, not talent, is the lever in US-China AI competition.
insights.quote: Oh, I heard an OpenAI average OpenAI researcher has 5,000 H100 equivalents that they can access at any time." and like their jaw just falls on the floor.

insights.claim: Lambert sees 20 to 30 companies building good models and calls the belief that only US labs can build models a form of cope.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Model building is less of a moat than many assume.
insights.quote: There's like 20 to 30 companies that are building good models.

insights.claim: The host notes the lag between open models and the frontier has shrunk to perhaps two to three months, pushing frontier labs to close APIs and favor first-party products partly to hinder distillation.
insights.speaker: a16z host
insights.so_what: Shrinking open-closed lag drives frontier labs toward walled-garden distribution.
insights.quote: now it's like maybe only two to three months.

insights.claim: Lambert expects Chinese labs to have more serious security than many assume because the Chinese government responds far more drastically to company misbehavior than the US does.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Contrarian view on Chinese lab security posture.

insights.claim: Distillation effectively converts money into compute-equivalent: knowing the outputs you want from a strong model is equivalent to having the compute to generate them.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Distillation is a compute-substitute for compute-starved labs.
insights.quote: outputs from a language model are a function of compute and if you know the outputs you want it's the same as having compute to generate with it with the model.

insights.claim: Lambert argues distillation mattered more in the SFT/RLHF era but maps poorly onto today's RL-heavy, environment-based post-training, so he believes it is not a huge effect in current post-training, albeit with big error bars.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Banning distillation would not erase Chinese progress.
insights.quote: previous post-training was much more reliant on the supervised fine-tuning

insights.claim: Evidence cited: fully open post-training researchers remain stuck using an outdated Qwen model because they cannot get distillation teachers right, and Lambert doubts Claude reasoning traces would have much improved Olmo.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Reasoning-trace distillation is technically harder than the narrative suggests.
insights.quote: all the open model builders are stuck using like a really outdated Qwen model because you can't figure out how to get the teacher right.

insights.claim: Lambert acknowledges suspicious activity supporting the labs' concerns: Claude proxies in China with many accounts and intermediaries, and cases of Kimi serving Claude inside its products.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Large-scale API abuse exists even if its training value is unclear.
insights.quote: even cases where Kimi was serving Claude in their products to users.

insights.claim: As long as frontier labs expose reasoning tokens via APIs, distillation cannot be stopped; restricting models to products and enterprise agreements would make it much harder, but Lambert opposes KYC mandates and government action over ToS violations.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Expect labs to self-secure via product gating rather than policy.
insights.quote: so long as they offer these APIs there's going to be no way to stop that type of distillation.

insights.claim: Lambert warns that federal action against Chinese AI firms over distillation would cause more harm than good, undermining US-China safety dialogue while not stopping the practice.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Policy crackdowns on distillation carry diplomatic costs with little effect.
insights.quote: I just think like you're going to cause more harm than good if you do anything about distillation cuz they're not going to stop.

insights.claim: Jensen Huang's framing that people distilling and dissecting his products every day is simply competition was raised as a counterpoint to anti-distillation rhetoric.
insights.speaker: a16z host
insights.so_what: Major industry figures frame distillation as normal competition.
insights.quote: People distill my products every single day. They take it and they they strip it down to its raw parts. They test everything. That's called competition.

themes.theme: Open vs closed economics and tiered markets

insights.claim: Lambert predicts tiers: best closed models command the best margins, while near-frontier models one step behind will be open, serving less profitable markets such as private enterprise data.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Margin structure will stratify by capability tier.
insights.quote: there's the best closed models which you can demand the best margins for. And then there's the near frontier models which is a step behind this. And those will be open

insights.claim: Fast following is structurally easy because data vendors sell datasets built for OpenAI and Anthropic to everyone else about a year later after contractual periods lapse; RL environments likewise reach Chinese labs ~6 months later.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Data vendors are a diffusion channel that erodes frontier lead.
insights.quote: those data companies a year later might sell them to everybody.

insights.claim: Open and closed models run on different exponential timescales: closed labs are integrated with efficient inference and revenue feedback, while the open ecosystem (builders, inference, post-training firms) lacks information flow and economies of scale, so it develops more slowly.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Open-model economy is slower but less bubbly.
insights.quote: I think open and closed models are on different time scales of exponentials

insights.claim: Enterprises adopting open models via fine-tuning partners like Thinking Machines or Prime Intellect end up with real ownership (weights, no ToS, own hardware, proven ROI), which Lambert sees as durable and less bubbly.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Post-training-as-a-service firms benefit from enterprise demand for ownership.
insights.quote: they have real ownership, which is model weights, no terms and conditions that they can run on their hardware

insights.claim: The host cites Cursor's SQLite-rewrite experiment where its Composer model with a frontier planner matched a two-frontier-model setup at far lower cost, as evidence open-source fine-tunes are good enough for many tasks.
insights.speaker: a16z host
insights.so_what: Fine-tuned open-based models can win on cost in agentic coding.

insights.claim: Lambert projects that if large model prices halve every 8 months for 3 years, costs reach about 1% within roughly four years, raising the question of whether Jevons paradox sustains margins or revenues fall.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Steep price deflation is a key risk/uncertainty for lab revenues.
insights.quote: reduce in price 2x every 8 months for the next 3 years.

insights.claim: Lambert is very confident frontier labs will serve the cheapest intelligence per watt/eval score and capture the highest-demand markets, but they cannot do everything, leaving room for the rest of the economy.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Expect many winners outside frontier labs' core markets.
insights.quote: So I'm very confident in the frontier labs being able to serve the cheapest intelligence per per watt, per score on an eval.

insights.claim: Lambert expected closed labs to win via Apple-like model-harness integration, but users' diverse harnesses forced all labs to support many harnesses, reaching an equilibrium; he expects open labs to follow on agent swarms once the shape is known.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Harness lock-in is weaker than feared; swarm coordination will diffuse.
insights.quote: it turned out that so many people have different harnesses for different things that they like to do

insights.claim: Frontier lab information security is weaker than they think; ideas spread over after-work chats, so labs' durable edge is inference infrastructure and margins rather than secret methods.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Secret-method moats decay in months; infra scale is the moat.
insights.quote: think like the the security at these labs in terms of information is not as high as they think.

insights.claim: Lambert believes much frontier progress in non-verifiable domains (knowledge work, biology, healthcare, legal) comes from buying high-quality data and environments rather than 'generalization magic', implying years of capital-intensive data buying across sectors.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Sustained demand tailwind for data/RL environment vendors.
insights.quote: a lot of the frontier progress in domains that are not fully verifiable is by buying data that is high quality and giving the models worlds to act in and hill climb on.

insights.claim: Lambert reads OpenAI's robotics jump as likely downstream of hiring and buying robotics data 6-8 months earlier, not pure generalization.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Capability jumps often trace back to targeted data purchases.
insights.quote: 6 to 8 months ago they started hiring people and buying a lot of data in robotics.

insights.claim: The RL environment boom has led vendors to cut corners, producing flawed data that induces reward hacking; labs buy in bulk with less than a 100% hit rate.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Quality-focused data vendors should win share as labs consolidate.
insights.quote: this RL environment explosion where there's just so much opportunity to make money is having a lot of people like like cut corners and this can induce things like reward hacking.

insights.claim: Labs are spending billions of dollars of research budget on environments, which Lambert takes as proof they see real model gains from them.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Environment spending is large and signal-backed.
insights.quote: The billions of dollars research budget on environments.

insights.claim: The data industry has low-hanging fruit in quality and opsec, e.g. overseas contractors via intermediaries uploading data to GitHub; Lambert expects a multi-year shakeout toward higher-quality, higher-ROI vendors.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Expect consolidation among data vendors.
insights.quote: There's a lot of stuff out there that if you poke around the data industry, you find weird rough edges.

insights.claim: Nearly all environment vendors sell synthetic data generated or modified by language models, even when humans guide the process.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Hand-built environments are rare; synthetic dominates.
insights.quote: All the companies are doing a mix of like all the companies are selling synthetic data

themes.theme: Trillium, open RSI and pretraining accessibility

insights.claim: Lambert's new nonprofit lab Trillium will mostly build open-source RL environments for high-leverage tasks, modeled on the fully synthetic TMAX terminal-task work that costs thousands to tens of thousands of dollars per environment.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Open environments could lower barriers for post-training research.
insights.quote: I think most of our work will be making open-source environments for tasks that are very high leverage.

insights.claim: High profit motives (nine-figure returns within five months of founding) pull researchers away from open work; Lambert joked such environment data could sell for $1M.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Commercial pull drains open research supply.
insights.quote: The opportunity to make uh what is $100 million like nine-figure returns for your business within five months of founding a startup

insights.claim: Trillium plans to demystify recursive self-improvement by publishing its full automation stack, tasks, configs and agent trajectories (using Claude, GPT, SkyRL, Miles) and checking in every 6 months.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Transparent RSI documentation may inform policymakers.
insights.quote: We're going to build an open-source stack for SFT, for mid-training.

insights.claim: Lambert expects AI to be very good at lowering serving costs and tweaking architectures, but not at solving general knowledge work soon.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Automated efficiency gains are near-term; knowledge work lags.
insights.quote: I do think the models will be really good at lowering serving costs.

insights.claim: Lambert argues a solid pretrained base model does not require $1B; tools like Megatron are open, and he does not bet against new entrants, though the hard part is landing a first model good enough to raise the next round.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Pretraining is not a capital moat; first-release execution is.
insights.quote: you don't have to spend a billion dollars to get a very good base model.

insights.claim: Thinking Machines got off the ground by transparently releasing Inkling and then a second model with Tinker; rumors suggest Meta will release open weights again.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: More open-weight supply may come from Meta and post-training firms.
insights.quote: There's rumors that Met- like Meta said they'll release a new open weight model again.

insights.claim: Post-training is now harder than pretraining for newcomers; long-context generation made architectural gains (e.g., sparse attention making 100k-token generation 40% faster) pay off, while open post-training lags so far that modest capital yields big gains.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Open post-training is a high-ROI area for capital.
insights.quote: it doesn't take as much capital to make very big compounding gains on the state-of-the-art in the open source cuz the bar is very low.

insights.claim: Lambert doubts a fast takeoff: scaling laws require exponential compute for linear gains and human bottlenecks remain; labs are spending exponentially more just to sustain progress, as some Claude system cards indicate.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Frontier labs cannot simply run away; open models can stay close.
insights.quote: The all the scaling laws are exponential increase in compute for linear increase in performance

insights.claim: Math is exceptionally well suited to current AI intelligence, but Lambert would update if AI discovered a fundamentally new architecture beyond the transformer.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Watch for AI-discovered architectures as a takeoff signal.
insights.quote: I'm of the opinion that math is exceptionally well suited.

insights.claim: Lambert's bigger worry is not capabilities but the near-nonexistent societal preparation, e.g. public cybersecurity, as capabilities diffuse from closed to open labs.
insights.speaker: Nathan Lambert
insights.so_what: Cybersecurity preparedness is an underinvested area.
insights.quote: But the AI capability plot in the pretty much non-existent preparation of cross public cybersecurity
